title: Folders Cannot Carry a Visual Collection
description: From 11 to 19 February 2026 the image collector gains a place in the work, a small vocabulary, similarity search, and captions that can run at a practical pace.
body:
A folder is a location. It is not a memory. Once a visual collection is larger than a person can browse, putting related frames in neighboring directories stops being a method. You are back to hoping someone remembers the name of the drawer.

This article covers the work from 11 February through 19 February 2026. It follows the collector of 8 February. The pictures already have hashes and a catalog. The question now is whether they can be found as evidence of work rather than as files on a disk.

Give the picture a place in the work

On 11 February the collector learns episode, scene, beat, and version, and it takes in more source roots than the original SwarmUI tree. That is not interpretation. It is a road sign: this frame belongs to a unit of work a person already knows how to walk. Most people browse. They follow episode and scene the way they follow a process folder. If the catalog cannot say where in the work a picture sits, later search will be a parlor trick on top of a pile.

On 13 February I add working categories for recurring production imagery — bins a classifier can actually use from prompt, filename, or folder. A vocabulary should help people locate and compare evidence without erasing what makes a frame distinct. These are small, testable labels, not a finished ontology and not yet a database registry.

Meaning, then a sentence, then speed

On 14 February the catalog is ingested into PostgreSQL with pgvector. One MiniLM vector per file, from the text the catalog already has. Related images can be asked for by meaning as well as by recorded fields. That is the same hybrid idea as the November index: exact structure plus similarity. It is still one vector per file. It is not a claim that the picture has been understood in several ways at once.

Prompts in PNG metadata are useful and incomplete. On 18 February a JoyCaption Beta One pipeline writes a natural-language caption into the search record beside the catalog evidence. Captions are sidecars. They do not replace the hash or the source path. On 19 February the pipeline becomes practical: CPU image loading overlaps GPU inference, with the GPU features this machine can actually use. A description that cannot keep up with the collection is a description that will not be run.

Each of those days is one move in the same argument. Narrative fields say where the frame sits in the work. Bins say what kind of recurring image it is. The vector says what it is like. The caption says what it looks like in a sentence a person could have written. None of those moves is allowed to discard the source path. If they do, we are back to a chat about pictures we can no longer find.

What this is not

There is not yet an entity registry. There is not yet a chosen authoritative source among several mirrors. CLIP is not in this path. Alfresco is not in this path. The test is whether a collected picture can be retrieved without walking folders. Until a first full run is measured, this is a working line from catalog to caption to vector, not a finished visual memory.

Historical basis: VALESKA commits 2549be7 (11 Feb), 10343d7 (13 Feb local), dd4f65a (14 Feb), 5d97e70 (18 Feb local), and d2929d4 (19 Feb). The article is dated to 19 February 2026, when the caption pipeline became practical. JoyCaption’s author timestamp is 18 February; 19 February is the UTC calendar date of that commit and the date of the prefetch work.
